title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
Likert-scale and rating-scale data are ubiquitous in educational and psychological research. Despite being ordinal (the distances between categories are not guaranteed to be equal), these outcomes are routinely analysed with linear regression or ANOVA — treatments that assume interval-level measurement and normally distributed residuals.
Cumulative link models (CLM) — also called proportional odds models or ordered logistic regression — respect the ordinal nature of the data by modelling the cumulative probabilities of response categories via a latent continuous variable and threshold parameters (Agresti, 2010; Christensen, 2019).
This project demonstrates:

CLM fitting on the wine dataset (ordinal package) — judges’ bitterness ratings of wines under different conditions.
Proportional odds assumption testing — verifying that predictor effects are constant across thresholds.
Threshold visualisation — interpreting the latent continuum.
Comparison with linear regression — demonstrating when the ordinal approach matters.
Simulated educational survey — ordinal modelling of student satisfaction ratings predicted by teaching quality and class size.

title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
0.2 Key Results
Part A — Wine tasting data (N = 72, 5-point bitterness scale):
Both experimental factors significantly predict bitterness ratings. Temperature (warm vs. cold) has a large effect: β = 2.503 (OR = 12.2, p < 0.001). Contact (yes vs. no) has a moderate effect: β = 1.528 (OR = 4.6, p = 0.001). The proportional odds assumption is supported for both predictors (nominal test: temp p = 0.365, contact p = 0.904). McFadden’s pseudo-R² = 0.166 — modest but within the expected range for ordinal data.
The comparison with linear regression confirms directional agreement (both predictors positive and significant in both models), but the CLM captures the ordinal structure: the OR of 12.2 for temperature means that warm wine is 12 times more likely to be rated in a higher bitterness category — a statement linear regression cannot make.
The partial proportional odds model (Appendix) confirms that relaxing the PO assumption for contact provides no improvement (LRT p = 0.904), validating the standard CLM.
Part B — Simulated survey (N = 800, 5-point satisfaction scale):
The satisfaction distribution is approximately symmetric (76/188/252/ 192/92), centred on “Neutral” — consistent with the symmetric generating thresholds. The CLM correctly recovers the direction and significance of both true effects (teaching quality: β = 0.959, p < 2e-16; class size: β = −0.586, p < 2e-16) and correctly identifies gender as non-significant (p = 0.711). The apparent coefficient inflation (~60%) is explained by the probit-to-logit scaling factor (π/√3 ≈ 1.81) — the generating model uses Gaussian errors while the CLM defaults to a logit link. After correction, parameter recovery is accurate.

1.2.1 Interpretation
The CLM output includes two types of parameters:

Thresholds (α₁|₂ = −1.34, α₂|₃ = 1.25, α₃|₄ = 3.47, α₄|₅ = 5.01): cut-points on the latent continuum separating adjacent bitterness categories. The increasing spacing between thresholds (Δ₁₂ = 2.59, Δ₂₃ = 2.22, Δ₃₄ = 1.54) indicates that the lower categories are more spread on the latent scale than the upper ones — it takes a larger shift in latent bitterness to move from rating 1 to 2 than from 4 to 5.
Predictor coefficients:

tempwarm β = 2.503 (OR = 12.2, p < 0.001): warm temperature massively increases perceived bitterness. The odds of being in a higher bitterness category are 12× greater for warm wine.
contactyes β = 1.528 (OR = 4.6, p = 0.001): grape skin contact increases bitterness, with odds 4.6× higher for the contact condition.


Both effects operate on the same latent scale — temperature has a roughly 1.6× stronger effect than contact on the log-odds scale (2.50/1.53).

Thresholds of the CLM model on the latent continuum (bitterness rating). Each vertical line marks the cut-off point between two observed categories.





1.3.1 Interpretation
The thresholds (α₁|₂ = −1.34, α₂|₃ = 1.25, α₃|₄ = 3.47, α₄|₅ = 5.01) divide the latent bitterness continuum into five observed categories.
The spacing reveals the scale’s measurement properties: - α₁|₂ to α₂|₃ (gap = 2.59 logits): the widest interval, meaning the model distinguishes well between “very low” and “low-moderate” bitterness. - α₃|₄ to α₄|₅ (gap = 1.54 logits): the narrowest interval, suggesting that ratings 4 and 5 are harder to distinguish — the top of the scale is compressed.
This pattern is common in sensory evaluation: judges use the middle of the scale more readily than the extremes, compressing the upper end.

title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
1.4 Proportional odds assumption

# ── Nominal test (relaxes proportional odds for each predictor) ──────────────
nom_test <- nominal_test(m_clm)
cat("=== Nominal Test for Proportional Odds ===\n")

=== Nominal Test for Proportional Odds ===

print(nom_test)

Tests of nominal effects

formula: rating ~ temp + contact
        Df  logLik    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>     -86.492 184.98                
temp     3 -84.904 187.81 3.1750   0.3654
contact  3 -86.209 190.42 0.5667   0.9040



1.4.1 Interpretation
The nominal test evaluates whether each predictor’s effect is constant across thresholds (proportional odds). A significant p-value indicates violation — the predictor’s effect differs depending on which threshold is crossed. If violations are detected, a partial proportional odds model may be needed (see Appendix).
Results: neither predictor violates the PO assumption (temperature: p = 0.365; contact: p = 0.904). The proportional odds hypothesis is well supported — the effects of temperature and contact are constant across the entire bitterness scale. This means a single coefficient per predictor adequately describes its effect, and the standard CLM is the appropriate model.
The high p-value for contact (0.904) is particularly reassuring: the effect of grape skin contact on bitterness is remarkably uniform across all rating thresholds.

title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
1.5 Further analysis of the model

# ── Modèle nul (intercept only) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
m0_clm <- clm(rating ~ 1, data = wine)

# ── CManual calculation of McFadden’s pseudo-R² ───────────────────────────────────
ll_full <- logLik(m_clm)
ll_null <- logLik(m0_clm)
mcfadden_r2 <- 1 - (as.numeric(ll_full) / as.numeric(ll_null))

# ── Tableau de diagnostics ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
diagnostics <- tibble(
  Metric                  = c("logLik (full model)", 
                              "logLik (null model)", 
                              "McFadden pseudo-R²", 
                              "AIC", 
                              "BIC"),
  Value                   = c(as.numeric(ll_full),
                              as.numeric(ll_null),
                              round(mcfadden_r2, 3),
                              round(AIC(m_clm), 1),
                              round(BIC(m_clm), 1)),
  Interpretation          = c("Likelihood of the fitted model",
                              "Likelihood of the model without predictors",
                              "Proportion of variance explained (0–1)",
                              "Information criterion (smaller = better)",
                              "Penalised information criterion (smaller = better)")
)

1.5.1 Interpretation
McFadden’s pseudo-R² provides an approximate measure of explained variation for the CLM. Values between 0.2 and 0.4 are typically considered good for ordinal data — a much lower threshold than the R² of linear regression, because ordinal models face a harder prediction task (categorical probabilities rather than a continuous outcome).
The comparison of log-likelihoods (full vs. null model) confirms that temp and contact jointly provide substantial predictive information beyond the intercept-only model. AIC and BIC can be used to compare this model with alternative specifications (e.g., partial proportional odds, additional predictors).
Our results :
McFadden’s pseudo-R² = 0.166 indicates a modest but meaningful improvement over the null model. For ordinal data, this should be interpreted differently from linear R²:

McFadden 0.2–0.4 is generally considered good for ordinal models (McFadden, 1974). The value of 0.166 falls just below this range, reflecting the fact that bitterness perception is influenced by many factors beyond temperature and contact (e.g., judge variability, wine composition).
Log-likelihood comparison: the full model (logLik = −86.5) is substantially better than the null (logLik = −103.7), a difference of 17.2 log-likelihood units — highly significant given only 2 predictor degrees of freedom.The comparison of log-likelihoods (full vs. null model) confirms that temp and contact jointly provide substantial predictive information beyond the intercept-only model. AIC and BIC can be used to compare this model with alternative specifications (e.g., partial proportional odds, additional predictors).
AIC = 185.0, BIC = 198.6: these serve as baselines for comparing alternative model specifications (e.g., adding judge random effects, interaction terms).

title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
1.6 Predicted probabilities

pred_grid <- expand.grid(
  temp    = levels(wine$temp),
  contact = levels(wine$contact)
)

pred_probs <- predict(m_clm, newdata = pred_grid, type = "prob")$fit
pred_df <- cbind(pred_grid, as.data.frame(pred_probs)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(temp, contact),
               names_to = "rating", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(rating = factor(rating, levels = levels(wine$rating)))

ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = rating, y = probability, fill = contact)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ temp) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(palette_ord[3], palette_ord[2])) +
  labs(
    title    = "Predicted Probabilities from CLM",
    subtitle = "Model-based estimates by condition",
    x = "Bitterness Rating", y = "Predicted Probability", fill = "Contact"
  )




Model-predicted probability of each bitterness rating by experimental condition.





1.6.1 Interpretation
The predicted probability plot translates model coefficients into directly interpretable quantities:

Cold/No contact (baseline condition): the distribution is centred on ratings 2–3, with very low probability of ratings 4–5. This is the mildest bitterness condition.
Warm/Yes contact (both effects active): the distribution shifts dramatically — the probability mass moves from ratings 1–2 to ratings 4–5. The modal category shifts from 3 to 4 or 5.
The CLM captures asymmetry: the shift is not uniform across categories. Moving from cold/no to warm/yes does not simply add a constant to the expected rating (as linear regression would imply) — it reshapes the entire probability distribution. Some categories gain probability mass while others lose it, mediated through the nonlinear threshold structure.

This is the key deliverable of ordinal regression: predicted category probabilities that respect the ordinal nature of the outcome. The statement “there is a 45% probability of rating ≥ 4 under warm/contact conditions” is directly actionable for winemaking decisions — something linear regression cannot provide.

1.7.1 Interpretation
The comparison confirms both agreement and divergence:

Agreement: both models detect the same direction and significance for both predictors (temp: p < 0.001 in both; contact: p = 0.001 in both). For binary significance testing, the two approaches give identical conclusions.
Coefficient magnitudes differ: CLM coefficients (2.50, 1.53) are on the log-odds scale, while LM coefficients (1.17, 0.67) are on the raw rating scale. They are not directly comparable, but the ratio is informative: temp/contact = 2.14 (CLM) vs. 1.75 (LM) — the CLM attributes relatively more importance to temperature.
Linear R² = 0.399 vs. McFadden R² = 0.166: these are not comparable — different metrics on different scales. The linear R² appears higher but is computed under the (violated) assumption that rating distances are equal.
Where CLM adds value: threshold-specific probabilities (see predicted probability plot above) and odds ratios (OR = 12.2 for temperature). Linear regression cannot make statements about category probabilities without additional distributional assumptions.

title: Ordinal Regression: Modelling Likert-Scale Outcomes
text:
2.1 Generate ordinal survey data

n_students <- 800

survey_data <- tibble(
  student_id      = 1:n_students,
  teaching_quality = rnorm(n_students, 0, 1),   # z-scored
  class_size       = rnorm(n_students, 0, 1),   # z-scored
  gender           = sample(c("F", "M"), n_students, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(
    # Latent satisfaction
    eta = 0.6 * teaching_quality - 0.3 * class_size + rnorm(n_students, 0, 1),
    # Ordinal response via thresholds
    satisfaction = cut(eta,
                        breaks = c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf),
                        labels = c("Very dissatisfied", "Dissatisfied",

2.2.1 Interpretation
The CLM on simulated data recovers the direction and significance of all effects correctly:

Teaching quality: β = 0.959 (p < 2e-16) — positive as expected. ✓
Class size: β = −0.586 (p < 2e-16) — negative as expected. ✓
Gender: β = −0.048 (p = 0.711) — non-significant, correctly detecting the absence of a true effect. ✓

The apparent “bias” is a scale artefact, not a model failure. The raw recovery table shows teaching quality estimated at 0.959 vs. true 0.6 (bias = +0.36) and class size at −0.586 vs. true −0.3 (bias = −0.29). Both are overestimated in absolute value by roughly 60%. This is expected and has a precise explanation:
The generating model uses a normal (Gaussian) error (rnorm(n, 0, 1)) with cut() thresholds — this is effectively a probit model. But the CLM uses a logit link by default. Logit and probit coefficients are not on the same scale: the logistic distribution has variance π²/3 ≈ 3.29 (SD ≈ 1.81), while the standard normal has variance 1. The scaling factor between probit and logit coefficients is approximately π/√3 ≈ 1.81.
Applying this correction:

Teaching quality: 0.6 × 1.81 ≈ 1.09 (expected logit coefficient) → observed 0.959 (within sampling noise).
Class size: −0.3 × 1.81 ≈ −0.54 (expected logit coefficient) → observed −0.586 (within sampling noise).

The “bias” disappears once the link function scaling is accounted for. This is a useful pedagogical finding: parameter recovery in ordinal models requires matching the link function to the generating process, or applying the appropriate scaling correction. In real data (where the true link is unknown), this is a non-issue — the logit coefficients are internally consistent and correctly interpretable on their own scale.

3.2.2 Interpretation
The partial proportional odds model relaxes the PO assumption for contact only, allowing its effect to vary across thresholds. The likelihood ratio test compares this flexible model with the standard CLM:

If the LRT is non-significant, the standard CLM is preferred (parsimony wins — the PO assumption holds).
If the LRT is significant, the partial model is justified and the threshold-specific coefficients for contact reveal where the effect differs.

This appendix demonstrates the workflow for handling PO violations. In the wine data, the nominal_test (Part A) did not flag any violation, so the partial model is expected to offer negligible improvement — but the code is ready for datasets where violations are detected.
Our results :
The partial proportional odds model relaxes the PO assumption for contact, allowing its effect to vary across thresholds. The results confirm what the nominal test indicated:

LRT: p = 0.904 — the partial model provides no significant improvement over the standard CLM. The 3 additional parameters (threshold-specific contact effects) are not justified.
AIC: 190.4 (partial) vs. 185.0 (standard) — the standard CLM is preferred by 5.4 AIC units, confirming parsimony wins.
The contactyes coefficient shows a singularity (NA) in the partial model. This is expected: when the PO assumption is relaxed, the overall contactyes coefficient is absorbed into the threshold-specific coefficients (1|2.contactyes = −1.62, 2|3.contactyes = −1.51, 3|4.contactyes = −1.67, 4|5.contactyes = −1.05). The relative stability of these values across thresholds (range: −1.67 to −1.05) visually confirms proportional odds — the effect is approximately constant, with only the 4|5 threshold showing a slightly attenuated effect.

This appendix demonstrates the workflow for handling PO violations: test → relax → compare → decide. Here, the evidence unanimously favours the standard CLM.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
text:
Reliability — the consistency of measurement — is arguably the most fundamental psychometric property of any assessment instrument. Without adequate reliability, validity evidence is uninterpretable, group comparisons are attenuated, and individual scores carry excessive uncertainty.
Yet the most commonly reported reliability coefficient, Cronbach’s α (1951), is widely misunderstood and frequently misapplied. Alpha estimates internal consistency under the assumption of essential tau-equivalence — that all items measure the same construct with equal true-score weights and uncorrelated errors. When this assumption is violated (as it almost always is in practice), α can either over- or underestimate true reliability (Sijtsma, 2009; McNeish, 2018).
McDonald’s ω (1999) provides a more general alternative. Omega total (ωt) estimates the proportion of total variance attributable to all common factors (without requiring equal loadings), while omega hierarchical (ωh) isolates the variance attributable to the general factor alone. The ωt/ωh distinction is critical for deciding whether a total score is justified or whether subscale scores should be reported (Reise et al., 2013).
This project demonstrates a comprehensive reliability analysis toolkit on the Big Five Inventory (BFI) dataset from the psych package (N ≈ 2,800; 25 items across 5 personality factors). We cover:

Cronbach’s α with bootstrap confidence intervals and α-if-item- deleted diagnostics.
McDonald’s ω — total and hierarchical, estimated via both the Schmid-Leiman decomposition and CFA (lavaan).
Split-half reliability with Spearman-Brown correction and all possible splits.
Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) and score confidence intervals.
Factor-specific reliability — per-subscale α and ω, revealing which factors are measured with acceptable precision.
SEM-based measurement quality — Composite Reliability (CR), Average Variance Extracted (AVE), Fornell-Larcker checks, and HTMT as an addendum for reflective CFA/SEM workflows.

The BFI is ideal for this demonstration because its 5-factor structure produces heterogeneous factor loadings (violating tau-equivalence) and correlated factors (complicating total-score interpretation), making the α/ω comparison maximally informative.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
text:
0.2 Key Results

Note: The results below are theoretical expectations based on published analyses of the BFI and the psychometric literature. They will be confirmed or refined once the code is executed.

Expected findings:

Cronbach’s α for the full 25-item BFI should be moderate (≈ 0.70–0.80), reflecting the multidimensionality of the item set. Per-factor α should vary: Neuroticism and Extraversion typically show α ≈ 0.80–0.85, while Openness and Agreeableness may be lower (0.70–0.75).
ωt (total) should exceed α because it does not require equal loadings. The difference (ωt − α) will be small if loadings are relatively homogeneous within factors, and larger if they are not.
ωh (hierarchical) should be substantially lower than ωt, because the BFI is designed to measure five distinct factors, not a single general factor. A large ωt/ωh gap confirms that the total score captures mostly factor-specific variance and that subscale scores are more interpretable than a total score.
Split-half reliability should vary across random splits, illustrating why a single split-half estimate is unstable. The Spearman-Brown corrected estimate should approximate α for essentially tau-equivalent scales.
SEM should be in the range of 2–4 raw score points (on a 25-item scale scored 1–5), translating to 95% confidence intervals of ±4–8 points around individual scores.
In the 5-factor CFA addendum, standardised loadings should mostly exceed .50, Composite Reliability (CR) should generally exceed .70, and AVE should be strongest for the clearest factors, with weaker domains occasionally falling just below .50 despite acceptable CR.

What to look for in the output:

The α vs. ωt comparison: how much does tau-equivalence violation matter for this dataset?
The ωh value: does a total BFI score make sense, or should subscales be reported separately?
The SEM-based confidence intervals: how wide are they? Are they wide enough to change practical decisions (e.g., classification)?
In the SEM addendum: do CR and AVE support convergent validity, and do Fornell-Larcker / HTMT suggest acceptable discriminant validity across the Big Five factors?

What we learn from analysing the dataset:
Part A — Data (BFI, N = 2,436 complete cases): After listwise deletion (87.0% retention) and reverse-scoring of 7 items (A1, C4, C5, E1, E2, O2, O5), the mean inter-item correlation is 0.093 — very low, confirming the strong multidimensionality of the 25-item set.
Part B — Cronbach’s α (full scale): Full-scale α = 0.698 [95% CI: 0.678, 0.716]. This value is substantially below the 0.80 threshold typically expected for individual-level use, but this is a diagnostic success, not a failure: α applied to a multidimensional scale is expected to be low and is not a meaningful indicator of measurement quality. The psych::alpha() function correctly flags items N1–N5 and O4 as negatively correlated with the first principal component — because Neuroticism points in the opposite direction from the other four factors at the total-score level. The α-if-item-deleted analysis confirms this: N4 (r_corrected = −0.106) and N5 (r_corrected = 0.013) would increase full-scale α if removed. This is the textbook scenario where full-scale α is inappropriate and factor-specific analysis is required.
Part C — McDonald’s ω: ωt = 0.879 (Schmid-Leiman), dramatically higher than α = 0.698. The gap of 0.181 — the largest in this project — reflects both tau-equivalence violation and the inappropriate application of α to multidimensional data. ωh = 0.475, yielding ωh/ωt = 0.54: the general factor accounts for just over half the reliable variance, confirming that subscale scores are more interpretable than a total score but that a general factor is not negligible.
CFA model fit is below conventional thresholds: CFI = 0.782, TLI = 0.754, RMSEA = 0.078, SRMR = 0.075. This is a well-documented limitation of the BFI-25: 5 items per factor is too few for strict CFA fit criteria (Soto & John, 2017). The model is adequate for demonstrating the reliability workflow but would require modification (e.g., correlated residuals) for publication-grade CFA.
Part D — Factor-specific reliability: Per-factor ωt ranges from 0.608 (Openness) to 0.820 (Neuroticism). Neuroticism and Extraversion (ω ≥ 0.77) are adequate for individual- level interpretation; Agreeableness and Conscientiousness (ω ≈ 0.73– 0.74) are borderline; Openness (ω = 0.608) falls short. The α–ω gap is minimal per factor (0.000–0.016), indicating that tau-equivalence violation is modest within each factor — the large full-scale gap is driven by multidimensionality, not by loading heterogeneity.
Part E — Standard Error of Measurement: SEM (ω-based) ranges from 2.37 (Agreeableness) to 2.57 (Extraversion), translating to 95% CI half-widths of 4.64–5.04 points on a 5–30 scale. This represents approximately ±17–20% of the scale range — substantial uncertainty for individual decisions.
Part H — SEM Addendum (CR, AVE, discriminant validity): CR values confirm the factor-specific ωt pattern (CR ≡ ωt, as expected). All AVE values fall below the 0.50 threshold (range: 0.257–0.485), indicating weak convergent validity — a known property of short personality inventories. The Fornell-Larcker criterion is violated for Agreeableness–Extraversion (latent r = 0.683 > √AVE for both factors), suggesting these constructs are not fully discriminable with 5 items each. HTMT values are all below 0.85, with the highest being A–E (0.646) — passing the conservative threshold despite the Fornell-Larcker violation.

text:
1.2 Reverse-score items
Several BFI items are reverse-keyed. We reverse-score them so that higher values consistently indicate more of the trait.

# ── BFI reverse-keyed items (from psych documentation) ───────────────────────
# A1 (-), C4 (-), C5 (-), E1 (-), E2 (-), O2 (-), O5 (-)
reverse_items <- c("A1", "C4", "C5", "E1", "E2", "O2", "O5")

bfi_scored <- bfi_complete
for (item in reverse_items) {
  bfi_scored[[item]] <- 7 - bfi_scored[[item]]  # Reverse on 1–6 scale
}

cat(sprintf("Reverse-scored items: %s\n", paste(reverse_items, collapse = ", ")))

Reverse-scored items: A1, C4, C5, E1, E2, O2, O5

After reverse scoring, all items keyed in the positive direction.

# ── Quick sanity check: inter-item correlations should now be mostly positive ─
avg_r <- mean(cor(bfi_scored, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")[lower.tri(cor(bfi_scored, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))])
cat(sprintf("Mean inter-item correlation (after reverse scoring): %.3f\n", avg_r))

Mean inter-item correlation (after reverse scoring): 0.093

2.1 Full-scale alpha

# ── Full-scale alpha with item diagnostics ───────────────────────────────────
alpha_full <- psych::alpha(bfi_scored, check.keys = FALSE)

probably should be reversed.

Cronbach's α (standardised): 0.719

Guttman's λ6:                0.803

Average inter-item r:        0.093

cat(sprintf("Signal/Noise ratio:          %.2f\n", alpha_full$total$`S/N`))

Signal/Noise ratio:          2.56



2.1.1 Interpretation
The full-scale α = 0.698 is low but entirely expected:

This is a multidimensional scale. The 25 BFI items measure 5 distinct factors, not one. Applying α to the full set treats them as unidimensional — a violated assumption that depresses α. The average inter-item r of 0.093 confirms this: items from different factors barely correlate.
The N-item warnings are correct. psych::alpha() flags N1–N5 and O4 as negatively correlated with the first principal component. This is because Neuroticism (high = anxious, unstable) points conceptually opposite to Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, and Openness (high = positive trait). Our reverse- scoring (A1, C4, C5, E1, E2, O2, O5) is correct within each factor — we should NOT additionally reverse N items, because within the Neuroticism subscale the items are correctly aligned.
Guttman’s λ6 = 0.803 is substantially higher than α, because it uses squared multiple correlations (SMC) rather than average inter-item r, making it more robust to multidimensionality.
Pedagogical value: This is the canonical example of when α misleads. A naive interpretation (“α < 0.70, the scale is unreliable”) would be wrong. The factor-specific analysis (Part D) will show that individual factors are adequately reliable.

2.2.1 Interpretation
The alpha-if-deleted diagnostic identifies items that weaken the overall scale:

Items above the dashed line would increase α if removed. In a multidimensional scale like the BFI, this is expected — items from one factor may correlate weakly with items from other factors.
Low corrected item-total correlations (< 0.20) suggest items that are weakly related to the total score. However, in a multidimensional context, this does not mean the item is “bad” — it may be an excellent marker of its own factor while correlating poorly with the other four.
This is precisely the scenario where α is misleading: applying α to a multidimensional scale treats all 25 items as measuring one construct, which they do not. Factor-specific reliability (Part D) will provide a more accurate picture.

In view of the analysis of the dataset:
The alpha-if-deleted diagnostic confirms the multidimensionality problem:

N4 (r_corrected = −0.106) is the only item with a negative corrected item-total correlation. Removing it would increase α from 0.698 to 0.720. This does not mean N4 is a bad item — it is the strongest evidence that full-scale α is the wrong metric. N4 measures Neuroticism well (CFA loading = 0.573) but correlates negatively with the total because the total is dominated by the other four factors.
All N items (r_corrected: 0.013–0.094) and O2, O4 (r_corrected: 0.106, 0.124) show weak or near-zero item-total correlations — consistent with items that are strong within their own factor but orthogonal to the general trend.
The strongest items for the total score are E3 and E5 (r_corrected ≈ 0.47), A2, A3 (r_corrected ≈ 0.44–0.45) — items from factors that happen to correlate positively with the first principal component.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
text:
3.1 Omega via Schmid-Leiman decomposition
The psych::omega() function estimates ωt and ωh by first extracting a factor solution, then applying the Schmid-Leiman transformation to decompose each item’s variance into general factor and group factor components.

# ── Omega with 5 group factors ──────────────────────────────────────────────
omega_result <- psych::omega(bfi_scored, nfactors = 5, fm = "ml",
                              plot = FALSE, n.obs = nrow(bfi_scored))

cat("=== McDonald's Omega (Schmid-Leiman) ===\n\n")

=== McDonald's Omega (Schmid-Leiman) ===

cat(sprintf("Omega total (ωt):        %.3f\n", omega_result$omega.tot))

Omega total (ωt):        0.879

cat(sprintf("Omega hierarchical (ωh): %.3f\n", omega_result$omega_h))

Omega hierarchical (ωh): 0.475

cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha:        %.3f\n", omega_result$alpha))

Cronbach's alpha:        0.823

cat(sprintf("\nωt − α = %.3f (tau-equivalence violation effect)\n",
            omega_result$omega.tot - omega_result$alpha))


ωt − α = 0.056 (tau-equivalence violation effect)

cat(sprintf("ωh / ωt = %.2f (proportion of reliable variance due to general factor)\n",
            omega_result$omega_h / omega_result$omega.tot))

ωh / ωt = 0.54 (proportion of reliable variance due to general factor)

text:
3.2 Omega via CFA (lavaan)
For a confirmatory approach, we specify the 5-factor CFA model and compute ω from the standardised loadings.

# ── Specify 5-factor CFA model ──────────────────────────────────────────────
cfa_model <- '
  A =~ A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5
  C =~ C1 + C2 + C3 + C4 + C5
  E =~ E1 + E2 + E3 + E4 + E5
  N =~ N1 + N2 + N3 + N4 + N5
  O =~ O1 + O2 + O3 + O4 + O5
'

fit_cfa <- cfa(cfa_model, data = bfi_scored, estimator = "MLR")

cat("=== CFA Model Fit ===\n")

=== CFA Model Fit ===

fit_indices <- fitMeasures(fit_cfa, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue",
                                       "cfi", "tli", "rmsea",
                                       "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper",
                                       "srmr"))
print(round(fit_indices, 3))

# ── Compute omega total per factor from CFA ──────────────────────────────────
compute_omega_factor <- function(loadings_vec, error_vars) {
  (sum(loadings_vec))^2 / ((sum(loadings_vec))^2 + sum(error_vars))
}

omega_per_factor <- std_loadings |>
  group_by(lhs) |>
  summarise(
    n_items     = n(),
    mean_lambda = mean(est.std),
    sum_lambda  = sum(est.std),
    sum_lambda2 = sum(est.std^2),
    .groups     = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    omega_t = sum_lambda^2 / (sum_lambda^2 + n_items - sum_lambda2)
  )

kable(
  omega_per_factor |> select(lhs, n_items, mean_lambda, omega_t),
  digits = 3,

3.2.1 Interpretation
The comparison of α and ω reveals key insights about the BFI’s measurement properties:

ωt > α: This confirms that tau-equivalence is violated — item loadings are unequal within factors. Alpha underestimates the true reliability when some items are stronger indicators than others.
ωh << ωt: The hierarchical omega is much lower than total omega. This means most of the reliable variance is captured by the five group factors, not by a general “personality” factor. A total BFI score (summing all 25 items) is poorly justified — the subscale scores carry most of the interpretable information.
The ωh/ωt ratio: Values below 0.50 indicate that less than half the reliable variance is due to the general factor. This is the key criterion for deciding between total scores and subscale scores (Reise et al., 2013).
CFA-based ω per factor: This provides the most accurate reliability estimate for each subscale, because it accounts for unequal loadings without the tau-equivalence assumption.

Our results :

ωt > α, but the gap varies by level of analysis. At the full-scale level, ωt (0.879) exceeds α (0.698) by 0.181 — driven primarily by multidimensionality. At the factor level, the gap shrinks to 0.000–0.016, indicating that within each factor, loadings are relatively homogeneous and tau-equivalence is approximately met. This pattern is maximally informative: it demonstrates that the α–ω discrepancy is not a universal constant but depends on whether the analysis is conducted at the appropriate level of aggregation.
ωh = 0.475, ωh/ωt = 0.54. The general factor captures just over half the reliable variance. This is a boundary case: the ratio is above the 0.50 threshold sometimes cited for justifying a total score, but only marginally. In practice, given the clear 5-factor structure and the poor full-scale α, subscale scores remain preferable for substantive interpretation, even if a weak general factor exists.
CFA fit is below conventional thresholds (CFI = 0.782, TLI = 0.754, RMSEA = 0.078, SRMR = 0.075). This is a known limitation of the BFI with only 5 items per factor — the strict proportional constraints of a simple-structure CFA are too rigid for personality items that often have minor cross-loadings. This does not invalidate the reliability analysis (ω is robust to moderate misfit) but means the CFA-derived indices (CR, AVE in Part H) should be interpreted with caution.
Factor-specific ωt (CFA) ranges from 0.608 (Openness) to 0.820 (Neuroticism). Openness is the weakest factor, driven by O4 (λ = 0.233) — an item that may be poorly understood by respondents or that taps a different facet of Openness than the other items.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
text:
4.1 Per-factor alpha and omega comparison

# ── Compute alpha per factor ────────────────────────────────────────────────
factor_names <- c("A", "C", "E", "N", "O")
factor_labels <- c("Agreeableness", "Conscientiousness", "Extraversion",
                    "Neuroticism", "Openness")

alpha_by_factor <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(factor_names), function(i) {
  items <- paste0(factor_names[i], 1:5)
  a <- psych::alpha(bfi_scored[, items], check.keys = FALSE)
  tibble(
    factor = factor_labels[i],
    alpha  = a$total$raw_alpha,
    mean_r = a$total$average_r
  )
})

# ── Merge with CFA omega ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
factor_rel <- alpha_by_factor |>
  left_join(
    omega_per_factor |> transmute(factor = case_when(
      lhs == "A" ~ "Agreeableness",
      lhs == "C" ~ "Conscientiousness",
      lhs == "E" ~ "Extraversion",
      lhs == "N" ~ "Neuroticism",
      lhs == "O" ~ "Openness"
    ), omega_t = omega_t),
    by = "factor"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    omega_alpha_diff = omega_t - alpha
  )

kable(
  factor_rel,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Factor-specific reliability: α vs. ωt"
)

rel_plot_df <- factor_rel |>
  select(factor, alpha, omega_t) |>
  pivot_longer(-factor, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = ifelse(metric == "alpha", "Cronbach's α", "McDonald's ωt"))

ggplot(rel_plot_df, aes(x = factor, y = value, shape = metric, colour = metric)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +

           size = 3, colour = "grey50", hjust = 0) +

  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Cronbach's α" = 16, "McDonald's ωt" = 17)) +
  ylim(0.55, 0.95) +
  labs(
    title    = "Factor-Specific Reliability: α vs. ω",
    subtitle = "Gap between markers = tau-equivalence violation effect",
    x = NULL, y = "Reliability Coefficient",
    colour = NULL, shape = NULL
  )




Reliability coefficients by BFI factor. Alpha (circles) vs. Omega total (triangles). The gap reveals tau-equivalence violation per factor.





4.1.1 Interpretation
The factor-specific comparison reveals:

Which factors are best measured: Factors with α and ω ≥ 0.80 provide scores suitable for individual-level interpretation. Factors below 0.70 should be interpreted cautiously at the individual level (though they may still be adequate for group comparisons).
Where α misleads most: Factors with the largest ω − α gap have the most heterogeneous loadings. For these, reporting α alone understates the scale’s reliability.
Practical recommendations:

Report ω (not α) as the primary reliability coefficient.
If ω < 0.70 for a factor, consider whether the 5 items adequately represent the construct or whether additional items are needed.
Report the SEM alongside reliability to communicate measurement precision in score-scale units (see Part E).


Taking into account the results of our analysis: 
The factor-specific comparison yields the project’s key insight:

Neuroticism (ω = 0.820, α = 0.817) is the most reliably measured factor, with the highest mean loading (0.685) and smallest loading heterogeneity. The α–ω gap of 0.003 confirms near-perfect tau-equivalence within this subscale.
Extraversion (ω = 0.767) and Conscientiousness (ω = 0.741) are adequate for group-level research (≥ 0.70) but fall short of the 0.80 threshold for individual decisions.
Agreeableness (ω = 0.732) is pulled down by A1 (λ = 0.344), which is notably weaker than the other A items (λ = 0.510–0.749).
Openness (ω = 0.608) is the clear outlier, below 0.70 for both α and ω. The problem is O4 (λ = 0.233) and to a lesser extent O2 (λ = 0.418). With 5 items, even one weak item substantially depresses reliability. If O4 were removed, the 4-item Openness ω would likely exceed 0.65.
The α–ω gap is negligible within each factor (0.000–0.016). This confirms that tau-equivalence holds approximately at the subscale level — the large full-scale discrepancy is entirely a multidimensionality artefact.

text:
5.2 Score uncertainty visualisation

# ── Hypothetical respondent at each factor mean ──────────────────────────────
mean_scores <- map_dbl(seq_along(factor_names), function(i) {
  items <- paste0(factor_names[i], 1:5)
  mean(rowSums(bfi_scored[, items]))
})

ci_df <- tibble(
  factor     = factor_labels,
  observed   = round(mean_scores, 1),
  ci_lower   = observed - factor_sem$CI95_half_omega,
  ci_upper   = observed + factor_sem$CI95_half_omega,
  SEM        = factor_sem$SEM_omega
)

ggplot(ci_df, aes(x = factor, y = observed)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
                  colour = "#2C3E50", size = 0.8, linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = "Score Confidence Intervals (95%, SEM-Based)",
    subtitle = "For a respondent at the sample mean on each factor",
    x = NULL, y = "Subscale Score (sum of 5 items, range 5–30)"
  )




Score confidence intervals (95%) for a respondent with mean subscale scores. Band width reflects measurement precision.





5.2.1 Interpretation
The SEM translates abstract reliability coefficients into concrete score-scale units:

A SEM of 2 points on a 5–30 scale means that a score of 20 should be interpreted as “somewhere between 16 and 24” at 95% confidence. This is a ±20% band — non-trivial for individual decisions.
Factors with larger SEM provide less precise measurement. When using these scores for classification or high-stakes decisions, the confidence interval should be reported alongside the point estimate.
Comparison with reliability: A factor with α = 0.80 and SD = 5 has SEM = 2.24; the same SD with α = 0.70 has SEM = 2.74. The 0.10 improvement in reliability translates to ~0.5 points of SEM — meaningful at the individual level.

Our results :
The SEM converts reliability into practical score-unit uncertainty:

SEM ranges from 2.37 to 2.57 across factors — a relatively narrow range, because the factors with higher reliability also have higher SD (the two effects partially cancel in SEM = SD × √(1−r)).
95% CI half-widths of 4.6–5.0 points on a 5–30 scale represent ±16–20% of the scale range. For a respondent scoring 20, the true score plausibly lies between 15 and 25. This band is wide enough to cross category boundaries in most classification systems.
Openness has the same SEM as better-measured factors (2.52) despite lower ω, because its SD (4.02) is the smallest. This illustrates why SEM is more informative than ω alone: a factor can have low reliability but still produce acceptable precision if score variability is also low.
Practical recommendation: For any individual-level decision (screening, selection, feedback), report the confidence interval alongside the point estimate. The SEM makes it impossible to ignore measurement uncertainty.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
text:
6.1 Random and systematic splits

# ── Split-half on Neuroticism (as an example factor) ────────────────────────
n_items <- paste0("N", 1:5)
n_data  <- bfi_scored[, n_items]

# ── Method 1: Odd-even split ────────────────────────────────────────────────
odd_items  <- n_items[c(1, 3, 5)]
even_items <- n_items[c(2, 4)]

r_odd_even <- cor(rowSums(n_data[, odd_items]), rowSums(n_data[, even_items]))
# Spearman-Brown correction (unequal splits)
sb_odd_even <- (2 * r_odd_even) / (1 + r_odd_even)

cat(sprintf("Odd-even split (Neuroticism):\n"))

Odd-even split (Neuroticism):

cat(sprintf("  Half-test correlation: %.3f\n", r_odd_even))

  Half-test correlation: 0.735

cat(sprintf("  Spearman-Brown corrected: %.3f\n\n", sb_odd_even))

  Spearman-Brown corrected: 0.848

# ── Method 2: Random splits (500 iterations) ────────────────────────────────
n_splits <- 500
sh_estimates <- numeric(n_splits)

for (s in 1:n_splits) {
  split1_idx <- sample(1:5, size = 2)  # 2 items in one half
  split2_idx <- setdiff(1:5, split1_idx)  # 3 items in the other

  r_split <- cor(rowSums(n_data[, split1_idx]),
                 rowSums(n_data[, split2_idx]))
  # Spearman-Brown for unequal lengths
  k <- 5 / length(split1_idx)  # full test / half test ratio
  sh_estimates[s] <- (k * r_split) / (1 + (k - 1) * r_split)
}

cat(sprintf("Random split-half (500 splits, Neuroticism):\n"))

Random split-half (500 splits, Neuroticism):

cat(sprintf("  Mean: %.3f\n", mean(sh_estimates)))

  Mean: 0.847

cat(sprintf("  SD:   %.3f\n", sd(sh_estimates)))

  SD:   0.035

cat(sprintf("  Range: [%.3f, %.3f]\n", min(sh_estimates), max(sh_estimates)))

  Range: [0.772, 0.880]

# ── Plot distribution of split-half estimates ────────────────────────────────
sh_df <- tibble(reliability = sh_estimates)

ggplot(sh_df, aes(x = reliability)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = palette_rel[4], alpha = 0.7, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(sh_estimates), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = alpha_by_factor$alpha[4], linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "#3498DB", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = alpha_by_factor$alpha[4] + 0.01,
           y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = 0,
           label = sprintf("α = %.3f", alpha_by_factor$alpha[4]),
           colour = "#3498DB", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "Split-Half Reliability Distribution (Neuroticism)",
    subtitle = sprintf("500 random splits — Mean = %.3f, SD = %.3f",
                        mean(sh_estimates), sd(sh_estimates)),
    x = "Spearman-Brown Corrected Reliability", y = "Count"
  )




Distribution of split-half reliability estimates across 500 random splits (Neuroticism subscale). The spread illustrates why a single split-half estimate is unreliable.





6.1.1 Interpretation
The split-half analysis demonstrates a key limitation of the method:

Split-half reliability varies by partition. With 5 items, there are only \(\binom{5}{2} = 10\) possible splits, but even this small number produces a range of estimates. The arbitrary choice of partition introduces instability — this is why α (the mean of all possible split-halves for standardised items) was introduced as a more stable alternative.
Spearman-Brown correction compensates for the shorter half-test length, projecting half-test reliability to full-test reliability. The correction assumes parallel halves (equal means and variances), which may not hold for all splits.
Mean split-half ≈ α: For essentially tau-equivalent items, the average across all possible splits converges to Cronbach’s α. Discrepancies indicate heterogeneous loadings (tau-equivalence violation) — consistent with the α/ω comparison.

title: Reliability Deep Dive: Beyond Cronbach’s Alpha
section: 8.1 Reliability and validity in SEM (Structural Equation Modeling)
text:
8.1 Reliability and validity in SEM (Structural Equation Modeling)
Important disambiguation: in Part E, SEM referred to the Standard Error of Measurement. In this addendum, SEM refers to Structural Equation Modeling.
This section addresses the user’s linked question directly: beyond α, ω, and the score-level SEM, researchers often evaluate measurement-model quality in a reflective CFA/SEM framework using:

Composite Reliability (CR) — a congeneric reliability coefficient based on the factor loadings and residual variances. In practice, this is conceptually much closer to ω than to α.
Average Variance Extracted (AVE) — the average proportion of item variance explained by the latent factor; commonly used as an index of convergent validity.
Fornell-Larcker checks — compare each factor’s √AVE with its correlations with other factors.
HTMT (heterotrait-monotrait ratio) — a complementary screen for discriminant validity.

These criteria are intended for reflective measurement models. They are not the right diagnostics for formative indicators.

library(semPlot)

semPaths(fit_cfa,
         what       = "std",        # standardised estimates
         whatLabels = "std",        # display standardised values
         layout     = "tree2",      # tree layout, factors on top
         style      = "lisrel",     # LISREL convention (ovals + rectangles)
         residuals  = TRUE,         # show residual variances
         intercepts = FALSE,        # omit intercepts
         nCharNodes = 3,            # abbreviate node labels to 3 chars
         sizeMan    = 5,            # observed variable box size
         sizeLat    = 9,            # latent variable oval size
         edge.label.cex = 0.65,     # edge label size
         fade       = FALSE,        # no fading by weight
         color      = list(lat = "#3498DB", man = "#ECF0F1"),
         border.color = "#2C3E50",
         edge.color = "#2C3E50",

text:
8.2 CR, AVE, Fornell-Larcker, and HTMT

# ── Standardised loadings and residual variances from the CFA model ──────────
std_sol_sem <- standardizedSolution(fit_cfa)

loading_df <- std_sol_sem |>
  filter(op == "=~") |>
  transmute(factor_code = lhs, item = rhs, lambda = est.std)

# ── Residual variances from standardised solution ────────────────────────────
# Under a standardised congeneric model: θ_ii = 1 − λ_i²
# This is algebraically equivalent to extracting diag(lavInspect(fit_cfa, "std")$theta)
# but avoids dependency on lavInspect's internal list structure, which can vary
# across lavaan versions.
resid_df <- loading_df |>
  transmute(item = item, theta = 1 - lambda^2)

factor_key <- tibble(
  factor_code = c("A", "C", "E", "N", "O"),
  factor = c("Agreeableness", "Conscientiousness", "Extraversion",
             "Neuroticism", "Openness")
)

# ── Construct-level SEM quality indices ──────────────────────────────────────
sem_quality <- loading_df |>
  left_join(resid_df, by = "item") |>
  group_by(factor_code) |>
  summarise(
    n_items      = n(),
    mean_loading = mean(lambda),
    min_loading  = min(lambda),
    CR           = (sum(lambda)^2) / ((sum(lambda)^2) + sum(theta)),
    AVE          = sum(lambda^2) / (sum(lambda^2) + sum(theta)),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(factor_key, by = "factor_code") |>
  mutate(
    sqrt_AVE     = sqrt(AVE),
    loading_flag = ifelse(min_loading >= 0.50, "All λ ≥ .50", "Some λ < .50"),
    CR_flag      = ifelse(CR >= 0.70, "OK (≥ .70)", "Low (< .70)"),
    AVE_flag     = ifelse(AVE >= 0.50, "OK (≥ .50)", "Low (< .50)")
  ) |>
  select(factor, n_items, mean_loading, min_loading, CR, AVE, sqrt_AVE,
         loading_flag, CR_flag, AVE_flag)

# ── HTMT from observed item correlations ─────────────────────────────────────
item_blocks <- list(
  Agreeableness     = paste0("A", 1:5),
  Conscientiousness = paste0("C", 1:5),
  Extraversion      = paste0("E", 1:5),
  Neuroticism       = paste0("N", 1:5),

R_items <- cor(bfi_scored, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

compute_htmt <- function(items_x, items_y, R) {
  heterotrait <- abs(R[items_x, items_y])
  monotrait_x <- abs(R[items_x, items_x][lower.tri(R[items_x, items_x])])
  monotrait_y <- abs(R[items_y, items_y][lower.tri(R[items_y, items_y])])

  mean(heterotrait) / sqrt(mean(monotrait_x) * mean(monotrait_y))
}

constructs <- names(item_blocks)
htmt_mat <- matrix(NA_real_,
                   nrow = length(constructs),
                   ncol = length(constructs),
                   dimnames = list(constructs, constructs))
diag(htmt_mat) <- NA

for (i in seq_along(constructs)) {
  for (j in seq_along(constructs)) {
    if (i < j) {
      val <- compute_htmt(item_blocks[[i]], item_blocks[[j]], R_items)
      htmt_mat[i, j] <- val
      htmt_mat[j, i] <- val
    }
  }
}

8.2.1 Interpretation
This SEM-based addendum adds a measurement-model lens to the earlier reliability analysis:

CR ≡ ω under the congeneric model. The Composite Reliability formula — CR = (Σλ)² / [(Σλ)² + Σθ] — is algebraically identical to McDonald’s ωt when both are computed from the same CFA standardised solution (Raykov, 1997; Peterson & Kim, 2013). Any convergence between Parts D and H is therefore expected and confirms computational consistency. The practical implication: researchers can report either CR or ω (or both for audiences from different traditions), knowing they estimate the same reliability parameter.
Convergent validity via CR and AVE. The conventional thresholds are CR ≥ .70 and AVE ≥ .50, alongside standardised loadings mostly ≥ .50 (preferably ≥ .70) (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Hair et al., 2022). AVE can be slightly conservative for short scales (5 items per factor), so a factor may show acceptable CR yet borderline AVE. That pattern usually means the construct is measured reliably enough overall, but some indicators are only moderately strong — a common finding with personality inventories where items sample diverse behavioural facets within a broad trait.
Discriminant validity — two complementary checks:

Fornell-Larcker criterion: the diagonal entries (√AVE) should exceed the off-diagonal latent correlations in each row and column. Violations indicate that two constructs share more variance with each other than each captures from its own indicators — a threat to construct distinctness.
HTMT: values below .85 provide conservative evidence for discriminant validity; below .90 is sometimes used when constructs are conceptually adjacent (Henseler et al., 2015). HTMT is generally considered a more sensitive criterion than Fornell-Larcker, especially when loadings are heterogeneous (Voorhees et al., 2016).

Integration with earlier findings. The Big Five factors are theoretically distinct but empirically correlated — especially Agreeableness–Conscientiousness and Extraversion–Agreeableness. If some Fornell-Larcker or HTMT checks are borderline for these pairs, this is a known property of the BFI rather than a measurement failure. The pattern should be interpreted in light of the substantive theory (personality dimensions are correlated, not orthogonal) and the brevity of the scale (5 items per factor limits the achievable AVE).
Best-practice caveat. No single index should be used as a dichotomous pass/fail gate. Modern guidance recommends combining CR, loadings, AVE, and discriminant-validity checks, ideally supplemented by bootstrap confidence intervals for HTMT and by examining the pattern holistically rather than relying on mechanical thresholding (Cheung et al., 2024).

Thus, SEM-based addendum adds a measurement-model lens to the earlier reliability analysis, and the results highlight the known limitations of the BFI-25:

CR ≡ ωt confirmed. The CR values match the CFA-based ωt to three decimal places (e.g., Neuroticism CR = 0.820, ωt = 0.820), confirming the algebraic identity under the congeneric model (Raykov, 1997; Peterson & Kim, 2013). This is not a coincidence but a mathematical necessity.
Convergent validity is weak. All five AVE values fall below the 0.50 threshold (range: 0.257–0.485). This means that, on average, each latent factor captures less than half the variance of its own indicators — the error variance exceeds the explained variance. This is a known property of short personality scales: items are designed to sample diverse behavioural facets within a broad trait, so they correlate moderately (mean r ≈ 0.25–0.47) rather than strongly. The CR ≥ 0.70 threshold is still met for 4 of 5 factors, creating the classic pattern “acceptable CR but low AVE” that signals reliable composites built from individually moderate indicators.
Openness fails both CR (0.608) and AVE (0.257). The combination of O4 (λ = 0.233) and O2 (λ = 0.418) depresses both metrics below any reasonable threshold. This factor would need revision — either replacing O4 or adding items — before use in an SEM context.
Discriminant validity — mixed evidence:

Fornell-Larcker violation for Agreeableness–Extraversion: the latent correlation (0.683) exceeds √AVE for both factors (0.605 and 0.633). This pair is not fully discriminable with 5 items per construct — a known concern with Big Five measures where A and E share variance through prosocial/interpersonal content.
HTMT is clean. The highest HTMT is A–E (0.646), well below the conservative 0.85 threshold. All other pairs are below 0.50. This illustrates why HTMT is often preferred over Fornell-Larcker: it is less sensitive to low AVE values that inflate the diagonal (Henseler et al., 2015; Voorhees et al., 2016).

Best-practice caveat. The poor CFA fit (CFI = 0.782) means all SEM-derived indices are conditioned on a model that does not fit well. In a publication context, one would either (a) improve the model (correlated residuals, exploratory SEM) before computing CR/AVE, or (b) report these indices with an explicit caveat about model fit. For this portfolio demonstration, the pattern is informative because it shows how to interpret imperfect results — a more valuable skill than reporting textbook-perfect numbers.



8.2.2 Practical reporting template
A compact SEM-style write-up for this dataset would look like:

For the reflective 5-factor CFA model, we evaluated construct reliability and validity using Composite Reliability (CR), Average Variance Extracted (AVE), the Fornell-Larcker criterion, and HTMT. CR values ≥ .70 were treated as acceptable evidence of construct reliability; AVE ≥ .50 and salient standardised loadings (≥ .50) as evidence of convergent validity; and discriminant validity was examined via √AVE-versus-latent-correlation comparisons and HTMT (< .85 conservative, < .90 liberal). These SEM-based indices complement the α, ω, and Standard Error of Measurement reported in Parts B–F, and are appropriate for reflective latent-variable models where both reliability and construct validity must be demonstrated jointly. —

title: Test Equating: Linking Scores Across Test Forms
text:
When multiple forms of a test are administered — whether for security rotation, longitudinal monitoring, or adaptive routing — raw scores on different forms are not directly comparable. A score of 25 on Form X may represent a different proficiency level than 25 on Form Y if the forms differ in difficulty. Test equating is the statistical process that adjusts scores on one form so they can be used interchangeably with scores on another, ensuring fairness and consistency in score interpretation (Kolen & Brennan, 2014).
This project demonstrates the complete equating workflow under the most common operational design: the Non-Equivalent groups with Anchor Test (NEAT) design, where two groups of examinees take different test forms that share a common subset of anchor items. The anchor items serve as the statistical bridge linking the two score scales.
We use the Kolen & Brennan benchmark data — two 36-item test forms with a 12-item internal anchor — accessed through two complementary R packages:

equate (Albano, 2016): provides the KBneat dataset as examinees × (total score, anchor score) for observed-score equating.
SNSequate (González, 2014): provides the KB36 dataset as item-level binary response matrices (1,655 + 1,638 examinees) with pre-estimated 3PL parameters, enabling IRT-based methods.

We implement and compare methods of increasing sophistication:
Observed-score methods (via equate):

Identity — no adjustment (baseline).
Mean equating — shift by the difference in means.
Linear equating (Tucker & Levine) — linear transformation preserving mean and SD relationships.
Equipercentile equating — nonlinear mapping matching percentile ranks, with log-linear pre-smoothing.

IRT-based methods (via SNSequate):

IRT parameter linking — mean-mean, mean-sigma, Haebara, and Stocking-Lord methods to place both forms on a common θ scale.
IRT true-score equating — mapping Form X expected scores to Form Y expected scores through the common θ scale.

title: Test Equating: Linking Scores Across Test Forms
text:
0.2 Key Results

Note: The results below are theoretical expectations based on the properties of the Kolen & Brennan data and the equating literature. They will be confirmed or refined once the code is executed.

Expected findings:

Mean and linear equating should produce similar concordance functions in the middle of the score distribution, with divergence at the tails. Linear equating corrects both location and spread, so it should outperform mean equating when the two forms differ in variability.
Equipercentile equating should provide the most flexible observed-score mapping, capturing any nonlinearity in the relationship between forms. With log-linear smoothing, the function should be smooth and stable.
IRT linking constants: The four linking methods (mean-mean, mean-sigma, Haebara, Stocking-Lord) should produce similar A and B constants. Characteristic curve methods (Haebara, Stocking-Lord) are generally more robust than moment methods (mean-mean, mean-sigma) when item parameters are estimated with error.
IRT true-score equating should yield a concordance close to equipercentile but with better behaviour at the extremes, because IRT extrapolates via the model rather than relying on sparse tail data.
Standard Error of Equating (SEE): Equipercentile SEE should be lowest in the centre and highest at the tails; linear SEE should be more uniform across the score range.

What to look for in the output:

The equating functions plotted together: how much do they diverge?
The SEE curves: which method is most precise at operationally relevant cut scores?
The IRT linking constants: do the four methods agree?
The difference between equated and identity scores: this is the practical adjustment magnitude.

FINDINGS (based on our dataset)
Part A — Data & Anchor Diagnostics (KBneat, N = 1,655 + 1,638): Form Y is substantially easier than Form X: the mean total score is 18.67 (SD = 6.88) vs 15.82 (SD = 6.53), a difference of 2.85 points. The anchor score difference is smaller (5.86 vs 5.11, Δ = 0.75), as expected since the anchor is a subset of the total test. All 12 anchor items show negative p-value differences (Group 2 outperforms Group 1 on every anchor item), with a mean |Δp| of 0.063 and an excellent cross-group correlation of r = 0.994 — confirming anchor stability and supporting the assumption that group differences are genuine ability differences rather than anchor instability.
Part B — Observed-Score Equating: The four equating methods produce meaningfully different concordances. At the mid-range (Form X = 15), mean equating yields 16.03, Tucker linear yields 15.98, Levine yields 15.42, and equipercentile yields 18.53. The equipercentile function applies a substantially larger and nonlinear adjustment: the difference-from-identity curve is not flat (ruling out pure mean equating) and shows curvature (supporting the equipercentile approach). Levine consistently gives the most conservative adjustment, while Tucker and mean equating are nearly parallel.
Part C — IRT-Based Equating: The four IRT linking methods agree reasonably: A constants range from 1.094 (Haebara) to 1.217 (Mean-Mean), and B constants from −0.458 to −0.557. Characteristic curve methods (Haebara: A = 1.094, B = −0.458; Stocking-Lord: A = 1.102, B = −0.477) agree closely, while moment methods show somewhat larger A values. The IRT true-score equating function shows a floor effect at low scores (Form X = 0 and 5 both map to 6.74 on Form Y) due to the 3PL pseudo-guessing parameters, which prevent the TCC from reaching zero. At mid-to-high scores, IRT true-score equating diverges noticeably from equipercentile (RMSD = 2.70, Max |adj| = 6.53), suggesting that the 3PL model and the observed-score distribution tell somewhat different stories — a finding worth investigating further.
Part D — Standard Error of Equating: Bootstrap SEE (200 reps) confirms the expected pattern: mean equating has the most uniform precision across scores, linear Tucker shows moderate increase at the tails, and equipercentile shows the most variable SEE with larger uncertainty at floor and ceiling.

text:
1.3 Score distribution comparison

# ── Build distributions directly from raw KBneat data ────────────────────────
build_dist_df <- function(scores, form_label, type_label) {
  tab <- table(factor(scores, levels = min(scores):max(scores)))
  tibble(
    score      = as.numeric(names(tab)),
    freq       = as.numeric(tab),
    form       = form_label,
    type       = type_label,
    proportion = freq / sum(freq)
  )
}

dist_df <- bind_rows(
  build_dist_df(KBneat$x[, 1], "Form X (Group 1)", "Total score (0–36)"),
  build_dist_df(KBneat$y[, 1], "Form Y (Group 2)", "Total score (0–36)"),
  build_dist_df(KBneat$x[, 2], "Form X (Group 1)", "Anchor score (0–12)"),
  build_dist_df(KBneat$y[, 2], "Form Y (Group 2)", "Anchor score (0–12)")
)

ggplot(dist_df, aes(x = score, y = proportion, fill = form)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Form X (Group 1)" = "#3498DB",
                                "Form Y (Group 2)" = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Score Distributions — NEAT Design (Kolen & Brennan)",
    subtitle = "Two 36-item forms, 12 common anchor items",
    x = "Score", y = "Proportion", fill = NULL
  )




Score distributions for Form X (Group 1) and Form Y (Group 2). Top: total scores (0–36). Bottom: anchor scores (0–12).





1.3.1 Interpretation
The total-score distributions reveal whether the two groups differ in overall ability — a key consideration for choosing equating methods. The anchor-score distributions should overlap substantially; large differences would suggest population drift or anchor compromise.
Examine:

Overlap of total scores: If the distributions are similar, the forms are roughly equally difficult and equating adjustments will be small. If one distribution is shifted, the equating functions will show a meaningful correction.
Anchor-score similarity: The anchor is the statistical bridge. If anchor distributions diverge, it may reflect genuine group differences (which equating should handle) or anchor item instability (which undermines all methods).

1.4.1 Interpretation

Key checks:

The anchor mean difference should be plausible (< 1 SD typically).

dataset

The anchor-to-test ratio (12/36 = 33%) exceeds the 20% minimum recommended by Kolen & Brennan (2014).

1.5.1 Interpretation
The scatter plot confirms excellent anchor stability: all 12 items fall close to the diagonal, and the cross-group correlation is r = 0.994. The consistent below-diagonal pattern (all p_diff values are negative) reflects the genuine group ability difference — Group 2 outperforms Group 1 on every anchor item — rather than item instability.
The largest deviation is A03 (position 9, Δp = −0.104), but even this item remains well within acceptable bounds. No items require exclusion from the anchor set. The mean |Δp| of 0.063 is modest, indicating that while the groups differ in ability, the items function equivalently across groups — the fundamental requirement for anchor-based equating.

1.5.2 Interpretation
Anchor item stability is a prerequisite for valid equating. Examine:

Points near the diagonal: anchor items function similarly in both groups — this supports the equating assumption.
Items far from the diagonal may exhibit DIF, compromising the anchor. If a few items are flagged, they can be removed from the anchor set (if the remaining anchor is long enough).
The correlation of p-values should be ≥ 0.95 for a well-functioning anchor. Lower values indicate instability.

Considering our results
The scatter plot confirms excellent anchor stability: all 12 items fall close to the diagonal, and the cross-group correlation is r = 0.994. The consistent below-diagonal pattern (all p_diff values are negative) reflects the genuine group ability difference — Group 2 outperforms Group 1 on every anchor item — rather than item instability.
The largest deviation is A03 (position 9, Δp = −0.104), but even this item remains well within acceptable bounds. No items require exclusion from the anchor set. The mean |Δp| of 0.063 is modest, indicating that while the groups differ in ability, the items function equivalently across groups — the fundamental requirement for anchor-based equating.

2.4 Equating function plot

eq_plot_df <- concordance |>

  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Identity" = "#95a5a6", "Mean" = "#F39C12",
                                  "Tucker" = "#3498DB", "Levine" = "#2C3E50",
                                  "Equipercentile" = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observed-Score Equating Functions — NEAT Design",
    subtitle = "Kolen & Brennan data: 36 items, 12-item internal anchor",
    x = "Form X Score", y = "Form Y Equivalent", colour = "Method"
  ) +
  coord_equal()




Equating functions mapping Form X scores to Form Y equivalents. The dotted diagonal is the identity (no adjustment).





2.4.1 Interpretation
Examine how the equating functions diverge from the identity line and from each other:

Where they agree (typically mid-range): all methods converge, confirming robust equating in the score region with most data.
Where they diverge (tails): linear methods extrapolate, while equipercentile is bounded by observed data. Tucker and Levine may diverge if the group ability difference is large.
Practical adjustment magnitude: the vertical distance from the identity line at key cut scores tells you how many points the equating corrects.

Considering our analysis
The equating functions diverge meaningfully, reflecting the ~2.85-point difficulty difference between forms:

Mean equating applies a constant +1.03 shift across all scores — the simplest correction, assuming the forms differ only in location.
Tucker linear applies a slightly steeper adjustment: less than mean equating at low scores (0.54 at score 0) and more at high scores (37.59 at score 36), reflecting the larger SD on Form Y.
Levine is the most conservative of the linear methods, producing smaller adjustments throughout.
Equipercentile diverges substantially from the linear methods, especially in the mid-range (score 15 maps to 18.53 vs ~16 for linear methods). This nonlinear pattern indicates that the score-to-percentile relationship between forms is not captured by a simple linear transformation.

The large divergence between equipercentile and linear methods is the most notable finding: it suggests the equating function is genuinely nonlinear, and linear methods would produce systematically biased equivalents in the middle of the score distribution.

2.5 Difference from identity

diff_df <- concordance |>
  mutate(across(c(Mean, Tucker, Levine, Equipercentile), ~ . - `Form X`)) |>
  select(-Identity) |>
  pivot_longer(-`Form X`, names_to = "Method", values_to = "Difference")

ggplot(diff_df, aes(x = `Form X`, y = Difference, colour = Method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Mean" = "#F39C12", "Tucker" = "#3498DB",
                                  "Levine" = "#2C3E50",
                                  "Equipercentile" = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Equating Adjustment (Difference from Identity)",
    subtitle = "Positive = Form X harder than Form Y at that score",
    x = "Form X Score", y = "Equated − Raw Score", colour = "Method"
  )




Equating adjustment (equated − raw score). Positive = Form X was harder at that score level.





2.5.1 Interpretation
This plot is the most directly useful for operational decisions:

Constant shift (flat line) = forms differ only in difficulty → mean equating suffices.
Linear trend = forms differ in difficulty AND spread → linear equating is appropriate.
Curved pattern = the relationship is nonlinear → equipercentile is necessary.
Large absolute values (> 2–3 points) suggest the forms are substantially different and equating is critical for fairness.

Our dataset :
The difference plot confirms that the equating relationship is not linear:

Mean equating produces a flat line at +1.03 — by definition.
Tucker and Levine produce gently sloped lines, reflecting the SD difference between forms (6.88 vs 6.53).
Equipercentile shows a pronounced curve: minimal adjustment at the extremes (< 1 point at scores 0 and 36) but a large adjustment in the mid-range (peaking at ~3.8 points around score 15).

This curved pattern has a clear psychometric interpretation: the two forms differ most in the middle difficulty range. Easy items (low scores) and hard items (high scores) produce similar proportions correct on both forms, but the medium-difficulty items are substantially easier on Form Y. A purely linear correction would undershoot in the middle and overshoot at the extremes.
For operational decisions with a cut score near 15–20 on Form X, the choice of equating method would change the equated cut by up to 2–3 points — enough to reclassify borderline examinees.

title: Test Equating: Linking Scores Across Test Forms
text:
3.1 IRT parameter linking
The KB36 dataset provides pre-estimated 3PL parameters for both forms. The 12 anchor items (every 3rd item) allow us to compute linking constants A and B that place Form Y parameters on the Form X scale.

# ── Extract 3PL parameters ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
parm.x <- KB36$KBformX_par
parm.y <- KB36$KBformY_par

cat(sprintf("Form X parameters: %d items × %d columns\n",
            nrow(parm.x), ncol(parm.x)))

Form X parameters: 36 items × 3 columns

cat(sprintf("Form Y parameters: %d items × %d columns\n",
            nrow(parm.y), ncol(parm.y)))

Form Y parameters: 36 items × 3 columns

cat(sprintf("Columns: a, b, c (3PL: discrimination, difficulty, guessing)\n\n"))

Columns: a, b, c (3PL: discrimination, difficulty, guessing)

# ── Anchor item indices (every 3rd item: 3, 6, 9, ..., 36) ──────────────────
anchor_items <- seq(3, 36, by = 3)

# ── Combine parameters for irt.link() ────────────────────────────────────────
# irt.link expects a data frame: [a_y, b_y, c_y, a_x, b_x, c_x]
parm_combined <- as.data.frame(cbind(parm.y, parm.x))
colnames(parm_combined) <- c("a_Y", "b_Y", "c_Y", "a_X", "b_X", "c_X")

# ── Run IRT linking ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
link_result <- irt.link(parm_combined, anchor_items,
                        model = "3PL", icc = "logistic", D = 1.7)

cat("=== IRT Linking Constants (Y → X scale) ===\n\n")

=== IRT Linking Constants (Y → X scale) ===

link_table <- tibble(
  Method = c("Mean-Mean", "Mean-Sigma", "Haebara", "Stocking-Lord"),
  A = c(link_result$mm[1], link_result$ms[1],
        link_result$Haebara[1], link_result$StockLord[1]),
  B = c(link_result$mm[2], link_result$ms[2],
        link_result$Haebara[2], link_result$StockLord[2])
)

kable(link_table, digits = 4,
      caption = "IRT linking constants: θ_X = A × θ_Y + B")


IRT linking constants: θ_X = A × θ_Y + B


Method

Mean-Mean

1.1689
-0.5155

3.1.1 Interpretation
The linking constants A and B transform Form Y θ-values onto the Form X scale via θ_X = A × θ_Y + B:

A ≈ 1 means the two forms have similar discrimination scales. Values deviating from 1 indicate that one form differentiates ability more sharply than the other.
B reflects the difficulty difference: positive B means Form Y was easier (Group 2 needs a boost to match Form X scale).
Agreement across methods: If all four methods produce similar A and B, the linking is robust. Large discrepancies suggest violations of assumptions (e.g., multidimensional DIF on anchor items).
Characteristic curve methods (Haebara, Stocking-Lord) are generally preferred over moment methods (mean-mean, mean-sigma) because they use the full item response functions rather than summary statistics.

Considering our results:
The four linking methods produce A and B constants in the expected pattern:

A > 1 for all methods (range: 1.094–1.217), indicating that Form Y’s θ scale is somewhat compressed relative to Form X — a unit of θ on Form Y corresponds to more than a unit on Form X.
B < 0 for all methods (range: −0.458 to −0.557), confirming that Form Y is easier: to place a Form Y examinee on the Form X scale, we subtract ~0.5 θ-units.

The moment methods (Mean-Mean: A = 1.217; Mean-Sigma: A = 1.169) produce larger A values than the characteristic curve methods (Haebara: A = 1.094; Stocking-Lord: A = 1.102). This is a typical pattern: moment methods are more influenced by outlier items with extreme parameters, while curve-based methods minimise the overall discrepancy across the full item response functions. The Haebara–Stocking-Lord agreement (A within 0.008, B within 0.019) supports the robustness of the curve-based linking.

title: Test Equating: Linking Scores Across Test Forms
text:
3.2 IRT true-score equating
With linking constants in hand, we transform Form Y parameters onto the Form X scale and compute true-score equating: for each θ, the expected number-correct on Form X is mapped to the expected number-correct on Form Y.

# ── Use Stocking-Lord constants (generally most robust) ──────────────────────
A_sl <- link_result$StockLord[1]
B_sl <- link_result$StockLord[2]

cat(sprintf("Using Stocking-Lord: A = %.4f, B = %.4f\n\n", A_sl, B_sl))

Using Stocking-Lord: A = 1.1020, B = -0.4770

# ── Transform Form Y parameters to Form X scale ─────────────────────────────
a_y_transformed <- parm.y[, 1] / A_sl
b_y_transformed <- A_sl * parm.y[, 2] + B_sl
c_y_transformed <- parm.y[, 3]

# Form X parameters (already on own scale)
a_x <- parm.x[, 1]
b_x <- parm.x[, 2]
c_x <- parm.x[, 3]

# ── Compute Test Characteristic Curves ───────────────────────────────────────
theta_grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.02)

# 3PL ICC: P(θ) = c + (1-c) / (1 + exp(-Da(θ-b)))
D <- 1.7

tcc_x <- sapply(theta_grid, function(th) {
  sum(c_x + (1 - c_x) / (1 + exp(-D * a_x * (th - b_x))))
})

tcc_y <- sapply(theta_grid, function(th) {
  sum(c_y_transformed + (1 - c_y_transformed) /
        (1 + exp(-D * a_y_transformed * (th - b_y_transformed))))
})

# ── True-score equating: map expected X score → θ → expected Y score ─────────
irt_equated_y <- numeric(37)

for (sx in 0:36) {
  if (sx <= min(tcc_x)) {
    irt_equated_y[sx + 1] <- min(tcc_y)
  } else if (sx >= max(tcc_x)) {
    irt_equated_y[sx + 1] <- max(tcc_y)
  } else {
    # Inverse of TCC_X: find θ such that TCC_X(θ) ≈ sx
    th_est <- approx(tcc_x, theta_grid, xout = sx)$y
    irt_equated_y[sx + 1] <- approx(theta_grid, tcc_y, xout = th_est)$y
  }
}
